title: Law Firms Navigate Unrelenting Challenges of Lateral Movement, Cyber Threats, AI Risks and Fraud — Ames & Gough 2024 LPLI Claims Survey (14th annual)
pub: Ames & Gough — 14th Annual Lawyers' Professional Liability Insurance Claims Survey
author: Ames & Gough

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source addresses lateral-hiring due diligence, portable-business claims and lawyer well-being, not the cluster’s proposition about multidisciplinary implementation, verification and task-specific evaluation of AI-enabled legal services. It therefore provides insufficient evidence to determine a position.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: Ames & Gough accepts the cluster’s supervised-use model, emphasizing lawyer competence, organisational training and security review rather than autonomous reliance. It materially extends the cluster’s confidentiality and governance analysis by framing AI exposure as a cyber and malpractice risk and recommending standalone cyber insurance, although it does not directly assess whether substantive verification consumes efficiency gains.
qs: Under this rule a lawyer cannot evade responsibility by claiming  to lack knowledge about how the AI system generally operates or how  its conclusions are reached.

Make sure your firm has a standalone cyber insurance policy that will cover  both first party and third-party cyber related claims so that your firm isn’t  exhausting its Lawyers’ Professional Liability Insurance limits and deductible.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s task-specific, risk-managed approach: it presents AI as useful for automating routine legal work while stressing confidentiality, privacy and malpractice safeguards. Its scope is narrower, however, because it focuses on law-firm use rather than direct-to-consumer access, users’ verification capacity or effective remedies.
qs: AI can not only automate and streamline manual, error- prone tasks but also augment how employees work which allows them to focus  on higher value tasks.
Attorney-client privilege and  work product protections still apply for data processed by AI, so lawyers must  maintain confidentiality and prevent improper disclosure.

st.t: Legal copilot: Verification costs define practical value
st.an: Ames & Gough supports the cluster’s cautious copilot framing: AI may streamline routine legal work, but lawyers remain bound by confidentiality duties and must use safeguards to control privacy and malpractice risks. It reinforces selective, governed adoption, though it does not directly assess hallucination rates or the cost of verifying substantive legal output.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core account of AI augmenting and automating bounded legal tasks rather than replacing lawyers wholesale, while emphasizing confidentiality, cybersecurity and responsible data handling as deployment constraints. Its treatment is narrower and does not materially address verification, apprenticeship or broader organisational competence risks.

st.t: Malpractice insurance: Reported AI claims remain hard to isolate
st.an: Ames & Gough directly supports the synthesis: it reports widespread insurer concern but only one observed AI-related malpractice claim, while documenting substantial broader malpractice severity that cannot be attributed to AI. It also favors supervised, risk-managed adoption rather than avoidance.

Claims paid over $100 million: Eleven of the 13 insurers (85 percent) have  participated in a claim payout in excess of $100 million in the last two years.

kp.k: Insurers fear AI risks, but reported claims remain rare
kp.d: Among 13 Lawyers’ Professional Liability insurers surveyed about calendar year 2023, AI was a leading concern for a majority, but only one insurer had encountered an AI-related malpractice claim. The document therefore presents AI risk mainly as an emerging exposure rather than an already widespread source of claims.
qs: Meanwhile, despite AI being a top line concern for the majority of the insurers we polled, only one insurer had seen an AI related legal malpractice claim whereas all of the insurers have seen an increase in cyber related legal malpractice claims.

kp.k: Insurers expect AI to improve legal-service efficiency
kp.d: The survey reports that most participating insurers see AI as beneficial because it may save time, reduce costs and decrease errors. The document predicts broad operational effects across law firms but does not quantify achieved productivity or cost improvements.
qs: Most insurers view AI as a benefit to the legal industry based on its ability to save time and reduce costs while cutting down on errors.
The significance of AI tools for law firms cannot be understated as they could change almost every aspect of how a firm may operate and conduct business.

kp.k: AI may automate review and augment higher-value work
kp.d: The document identifies bill review, case-document review and contract-clause identification as tasks AI can support or automate. Its framing is principally copilot-like augmentation—an AI assistant checking work and allowing employees to concentrate on higher-value tasks—although it also anticipates automation of work currently performed by employees.
qs: For example, while an experienced contract lawyer already knows how to find obscure clauses, it can’t hurt to have an AI “assistant” looking over the attorney’s shoulder, finding clauses the attorney may have missed.
Incorporating AI technology can empower firms to run more efficiently and economically by automating many tasks currently performed by employees (such as bill and case document review).
AI can not only automate and streamline manual, error- prone tasks but also augment how employees work which allows them to focus on higher value tasks.

kp.k: Confidentiality dominates the identified AI malpractice exposure
kp.d: The document links generative-AI use to possible disclosure of privileged, work-product and other confidential information, particularly when lawyers submit case-specific data to third-party systems. It recommends considering anonymised or redacted inputs and understanding platform security and data-retention practices.
qs: Despite all of the potential benefits of AI for the firm’s bottom line, there is some apprehension on the potential for privacy breaches as lawyers start to use generative AI to help answer a specific legal question or draft a document specific to a case.
Attorney-client privilege and work product protections still apply for data processed by AI, so lawyers must maintain confidentiality and prevent improper disclosure.
When entering data into machine learning systems, lawyers may want to consider only providing anonymous or redacted documents.
The reality is that law firms may accidentally share confidential information with third parties, such as a platform developer or other users of an AI platform without even knowing it.

kp.k: Technology competence requires lawyers to understand AI risks
kp.d: The document applies ABA Model Rule 1.1 Comment 8’s technology-competence principle to AI. It argues that lawyers must understand AI sufficiently to assess client and practice risks and cannot avoid responsibility by professing ignorance of system operation or outputs.
qs: Competence: ABA Model Rule 1.1 Comment 8 requires lawyers to maintain the requisite knowledge and skill to be competitive and “keep abreast of any changes in the law and its practice,” including the benefits and risks associated with relevant technology.
This includes understanding AI enough to understand any risks it may pose to their clients and their practice.
Under this rule a lawyer cannot evade responsibility by claiming to lack knowledge about how the AI system generally operates or how its conclusions are reached.

Firms should take measures to appreciate the operative security policies of the AI system it is using, including any encryption technology and the extent to which documents are retained and how long they are preserved.

kp.k: AI use may require client disclosure and consent
kp.d: Applying ABA Model Rule 1.4, the document states that lawyers’ communication duties extend to technology used in a representation. Depending on the circumstances, lawyers may need to explain AI use, obtain informed consent and notify clients if their information is materially lost or compromised.
qs: Communication: ABA Model Rule 1.4 applies to attorneys’ use of technology.
It requires appropriate communications with clients “about the means by which the client’s objectives are to be accomplished,” including the use of technology.
It requires keeping the client informed and, depending on the circumstances, may require obtaining “informed consent” about use of technology.
It requires notice to a client of a material loss or compromise of information relating to the client.

kp.k: Lawyers must supervise and train organizational AI users
kp.d: The document applies the supervisory duties in ABA Model Rules 5.1 and 5.3 to AI use by lawyers and non-lawyers. It recommends ensuring that organizational users understand the ethical implications and receive proper training, preserving lawyer oversight of technology-assisted work.
qs: Supervision: ABA Model Rules 5.1 and 5.3 state that attorneys have a duty to supervise lawyers and non-lawyers working with them.
Attorneys should ensure that those in their organization using AI understand the ethical considerations surrounding its use and are properly trained on its usage.

kp.k: AI-specific regulation must keep pace with technological change
kp.d: The document calls for AI-specific legal and ethical responses to rapid technological development. This is a recommendation about regulatory adaptation rather than evidence that existing professional standards have already been comprehensively replaced or revised.
qs: In the interim, there is a growing urgency to tackle AI-specific laws and to make sure the ethical standards placed on the legal industry can keep pace with the rapid enhancements in technology.

kp.k: Large firms are deploying AI for routine workplace tasks
kp.d: As an adoption example, the document reports that Clifford Chance announced in February 2024 a firm-wide partnership with Microsoft involving AI-powered workplace solutions. The anticipated uses included document summaries, minute-taking and email drafting; these are the chief technology officer’s hoped-for applications, not measured outcomes.
qs: Some firms have raced further ahead than others in the use of AI tools.
In February this year, for example, Clifford Chance announced it had partnered with tech giant Microsoft to roll out a “holistic suite of AI-powered workplace solutions” across the whole firm.
According to an interview with Law360, the firm’s chief technology officer hoped the tool will help across a variety of tasks such as summarizing documents, recording minutes, and drafting emails.

kp.k: Insurers resist covering AI losses under malpractice policies
kp.d: The document states that legal-malpractice insurers do not want Lawyers’ Professional Liability policies to absorb AI- and cyber-related losses. It recommends standalone cyber coverage for first- and third-party claims so firms do not exhaust their professional-liability limits and deductible.
qs: In summary, legal malpractice insurers do not want to cover AI and cyber- related losses under the Lawyers’ Professional Liability insurance policy.

Make sure your firm has a standalone cyber insurance policy that will cover both first party and third-party cyber related claims so that your firm isn’t exhausting its Lawyers’ Professional Liability Insurance limits and deductible.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Ames & Gough reports that most surveyed insurers regard AI as beneficial and argues that automation and lawyer augmentation could change nearly every aspect of law-firm operations.
pts.d: The benefits attributed to most insurers are time savings, cost reductions and fewer errors. Ames & Gough illustrates augmentation with an AI assistant identifying contract clauses an experienced lawyer might miss. It also predicts greater operational efficiency through automating bill and case-document review and enabling employees to concentrate on higher-value tasks. These are potential benefits, not measured productivity findings; the report does not predict job losses.

pts.k: Ames & Gough identifies confidentiality breaches and resulting malpractice exposure as risks of using generative AI for legal questions and case-specific drafting.
pts.d: The report says firms may unknowingly disclose confidential information to platform developers or other users. It maintains that privilege and work-product protections continue to apply to AI-processed data and warns that insufficient attention to AI and cybersecurity threats increases malpractice risk. Its suggested safeguards include anonymous or redacted inputs and scrutiny of AI-system security and document-retention policies.

pts.k: Ames & Gough argues that AI use entails continuing lawyer responsibility, technology competence, client communication and supervision rather than transferring responsibility to the system.
pts.d: Drawing on ABA Model Rules, the report says lawyers must understand AI risks, cannot disclaim responsibility through ignorance of how the system works, and should train and supervise personnel using AI. Client communication may, depending on circumstances, require informed consent. It also expresses urgency about AI-specific laws and ethical standards keeping pace with technological advances. These are the report's interpretations and recommendations, not findings of newly enacted AI-specific duties.

pts.k: AI was a major insurer concern despite limited reported AI-related claims; Ames & Gough says insurers do not want AI and cyber losses covered under professional-liability policies.
pts.d: Only one surveyed insurer reported having seen an AI-related legal-malpractice claim. This counts insurers reporting exposure, not individual claims or a market-wide incidence rate. Ames & Gough separately asserts an insurer preference against covering AI and cyber losses under lawyers' professional-liability insurance and recommends standalone cyber coverage to preserve professional-liability limits and deductibles. It does not supply policy language or establish that all AI-related losses would be covered by a cyber policy.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of insurer survey responses, illustrative use cases, professional-rule authority and a reported firm deployment—not AI performance benchmarks.
pts.d: The 2024 survey covers 13 leading professional-liability insurers that together insure more than 80 percent of AM Law 250 firms. It supports the reported insurer attitudes and the observation that one insurer had seen an AI-related claim, but provides no details about that claim. Efficiency and error-reduction claims are supported by insurer views and hypothetical workflow examples, not quantified tests. Ethical guidance invokes ABA Model Rules, including Rule 1.1 Comment 8, Rule 1.4, Rule 1.6 and supervision rules. As an adoption example, Ames & Gough reports Clifford Chance's February 2024 Microsoft rollout; expected task benefits are attributed to its chief technology officer, as reported in a Law360 interview, rather than presented as demonstrated results.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The survey reports on 2023, with adoption commentary extending into 2024; operational transformation is prospective and has no specified completion date.
pts.d: The report presents AI concerns and limited claims experience as current survey observations, without dating the individual AI-related claim. The Clifford Chance example concerns February 2024. Broad benefits are qualified by language such as 'could,' 'can' and the technology officer's 'hoped.' Privacy risks arise when lawyers submit client or case information to AI platforms; elevated malpractice risk is conditional on insufficient attention to threats. Informed consent is expressly circumstance-dependent, and the report notes uneven adoption across firms.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims concern law firms, practicing lawyers and employees, their clients, and professional-liability insurers.
pts.d: Firms may gain efficiency and bottom-line benefits but face security, governance and insurance-management demands. Contract lawyers may receive assistance identifying clauses; employees performing routine review may shift attention to higher-value work. Lawyers retain responsibility for AI use and supervision. Clients face possible exposure of confidential information and may need communication or consent regarding technology use. Insurers face emerging AI-related malpractice exposure. The survey has substantial large-firm insurance coverage, but Ames & Gough frames its guidance for law firms generally; it makes no specific AI claim about access to justice, ALSP competition, pricing models or staffing reductions.
